result: Human cells contain one FTS, three Hook proteins (Hook1, Hook2, Hook3), and four FHIP proteins (FHIP1A, FHIP1B, FHIP2A, FHIP2B), which are components of the dynein motor system that organizes intracellular transport.
evaluation: Claims C1-C6 establish the basic composition of the FHF complex in human cells. The phylogenetic analysis (Figure 1B) and established knowledge about dynein and kinesin motors provide strong support for these foundational claims about protein composition.

result: Different FHIP proteins preferentially associate with specific Hook proteins: FHIP1A and FHIP1B interact with Hook1 and Hook3, while FHIP2A preferentially interacts with Hook2, and FHIP2B can interact with all three Hook proteins.
evaluation: Claims C7-C15 and C106 are well-supported by converging evidence from BioID proximity labeling (Figures 1C, 2A) and reciprocal coimmunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A). The data consistently show preferential Hook-FHIP interactions, though some promiscuity exists (e.g., FHIP2B with all Hooks).

result: Hook2 is a bona fide dynein activating adaptor that, in the presence of Lis1, activates processive dynein/dynactin motility in vitro with similar speeds to Hook3-activated complexes.
evaluation: Claims C16-C19, C87, and C88 are supported by single-molecule motility assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The ~threefold increase in processive runs with Lis1 and similar velocities between Hook2 and Hook3 complexes provide strong evidence. This is the first demonstration that Hook2 activates dynein motility in vitro.

result: Different FHF complexes (FTS/Hook2/FHIP2A and FTS/Hook3/FHIP1B) associate with moving dynein/dynactin complexes in vitro, with minimal effects on dynein motile properties, and no other proteins are required for complex formation or movement.
evaluation: Claims C20-C27 and C86 are supported by in vitro reconstitution experiments showing colocalization of fluorescently labeled FHF components with moving dynein (Figure 3B-C). Controls lacking Hook proteins show no colocalization (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-B). The minimal effects on velocity, landing rates, and pausing frequencies demonstrate that FHF complexes do not significantly alter dynein's intrinsic motility.

result: FHIP1B and FHIP2A associate with motile cargos on microtubules but with distinct morphologies: FHIP1B associates with punctate structures while FHIP2A associates with both punctate and tubular structures.
evaluation: Claims C28-C29 and C107-C109 are supported by live-cell spinning-disk confocal imaging (Figure 4C-F, Videos 1-2). The distinct morphologies suggest different cargo specificities, consistent with the BioID interactome differences.

result: FHIP1B is a Rab5-specific effector that directly binds GTP-bound Rab5B and, together with Hook1 and/or Hook3, links dynein to Rab5B-marked early endosomes, driving their transport toward microtubule minus ends near the centrosome.
evaluation: Claims C30-C37, C72-C73, C78, C90, C125, C128-C129 are strongly supported by multiple lines of evidence: live-cell imaging showing FHIP1B/Rab5B colocalization (Figure 5B-C, Videos 3-6), immunofluorescence (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), centrosomal accumulation upon FHIP1B overexpression (Figure 5D), direct binding assays showing preferential interaction with GMPPNP-bound Rab5B (Figure 5F), and specificity demonstrated by coimmunoprecipitation with Rab5B but not 12 other Rab GTPases (Figure 5G).

result: FHIP2A, together with Hook2, links dynein to Rab1A-associated ER-to-Golgi tubular transport intermediates and is involved in the motility (rather than formation) of Rab1A tubules, though the FHIP2A-Rab1A interaction is likely indirect.
evaluation: Claims C38-C44, C70-C71, C74-C76, C79-C81, C110, C126, C130-C131 are supported by multiple experiments: colocalization with ER-to-Golgi markers (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), strong colocalization with Rab1A but not other GTPases (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A), colocalization with VSV-G tubules during ER-to-Golgi transport (Figure 6B, Video 7), Hook2 colocalization with Rab1A (Videos 8-10), dependence on GTP-bound Rab1A (Figure 7A-B), and rescue of motile tubule numbers in FHIP2A KO cells (Figure 7D). The lack of direct coimmunoprecipitation (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A-B) suggests an indirect interaction.

result: The presence of membrane-bound (GTP-loaded) Rab1A on ER-to-Golgi tubules is linked to FHIP2A recruitment, and FHIP2A knockout reduces the number of motile Rab1A tubules by 39%, which is rescued by FHIP2A re-expression.
evaluation: Claims C45-C51 are supported by experiments with Rab1A mutants (Figure 7A-B) showing that wild-type and GTP-locked Rab1A support motile tubules with FHIP2A colocalization (≥73% of cells with >5 motile tubules), while GDP-locked Rab1A does not (0% for Rab1A, 22% for FHIP2A). The FHIP2A KO phenotype and rescue (Figure 7D) demonstrate functional importance. The slight decrease in tubule length in KO cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) supports a primary role in motility.

result: Different FHIP proteins have distinct BioID interactomes: FHIP1A/1B are enriched for endosome-associated proteins, FHIP2A/2B for Golgi-associated proteins (with FHIP2A specific for ER-to-Golgi transport and FHIP2B enriched for mitochondria-associated proteins), suggesting FHIP proteins are the most cargo-proximal components of FHF complexes.
evaluation: Claims C82-C84, C95-C101 are supported by comprehensive BioID mass spectrometry data (Figure 1C, Supplementary files 1-2). The distinct interactomes with limited overlap between different FHIPs, combined with the proximity-dependent nature of BioID, strongly support the conclusion that FHIPs are cargo-proximal adaptors. GO analysis confirms enrichment of functionally related proteins in each dataset.

result: Combinatorial assembly of different FTS-Hook-FHIP complexes, enabled by gene expansion and functional divergence of Hook and FHIP protein families, provides a mechanism for dynein to achieve cargo specificity.
evaluation: Claims C67-C69, C85, C122-C124 represent the central conclusion of the manuscript. This is well-supported by the totality of evidence showing: (1) preferential Hook-FHIP interactions, (2) distinct cargo associations for different FHF complexes, (3) in vitro reconstitution demonstrating sufficiency of purified components, and (4) functional validation through knockout/rescue experiments. The model is illustrated in Figure 8.

result: FHIP1A and FHIP1B show partial redundancy but may have distinct functions (e.g., FHIP1A in TFR recycling), FHIP2B may function in endosome-to-Golgi transport or mitochondrial transport, and the FHIP/Hook interactomes provide a resource for identifying additional dynein cargos.
evaluation: Claims C91-C94, C115-C121 are largely speculative or represent future directions. While the BioID data showing shared and unique hits are valid (e.g., TFR and sorting nexins in FHIP1A, mitochondrial proteins in FHIP2B), the functional interpretations are not experimentally validated in this study. The statement about the resource value (C120-C121) is reasonable but represents potential rather than demonstrated utility.

result: Prior work has established that FHF complexes link dynein to cargo in fungi and mammals, that dynein requires dynactin and activating adaptors for processive motility, and that various adaptors link dynein to Rab GTPases, though the mechanisms are incompletely understood.
evaluation: Claims C52-C66, C104-C105, C111-C114, C127, C132-C139 represent background knowledge and prior work cited in the manuscript. These are appropriately cited and provide context for the current study. The absence of HOPS complex components in the authors' FHIP datasets (C105) contrasts with prior reports (C104), which is noted but not fully resolved.

result: Rab5B was detected in the FHIP1B BioID dataset, and it is possible that FHF complexes containing FHIP1B/Hook1 versus FHIP1B/Hook3 may interact with different subpopulations of endosomes.
evaluation: Claim C102 is directly supported by the BioID data. Claim C140 is speculative but reasonable given that Hook1 (but not Hook3) was previously shown to colocalize with a subpopulation of Rab5-marked endosomes in neurons (cited as Olenick et al., 2019). However, this hypothesis is not tested in the current manuscript.
